To imitate the spouse's handwriting, the narrator rehearsed that line repeatedly, producing seven practice copies. The seven repetitions themselves are the damning evidence: they show the narrator deliberately rehearsing the exact phrase used in the fake note, exposing the forgery and thus the murder. The closing "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble" is the narrator realizing that this handwriting practice will reveal what they did.

runs.latest_final: A human (the narrator) speaks the sentence "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" aloud to one other human, and it is shown repeated for emphasis rather than as a meaningful count. The person addressed is blameless — they did nothing to deserve the accusation of disappointing the narrator. Saying the line is not itself what creates the impending consequences; the narrator is simultaneously engaged in some separate wrongdoing, and it is that act, not the farewell, that will bring trouble. The narrator knows this: the "trouble" is a future, serious (not playful, not mere physical danger) consequence they anticipate. The lament serves as a deflection or self-justifying send-off spoken while the real transgression is underway, and the sigh "I know I'm in trouble" acknowledges that the coming reckoning stems from the concealed wrongful act rather than from the words themselves.

runs.latest_final: A man has killed his wife/partner. To cover up the death and make it look as though she simply walked out on him, he writes a farewell note in her voice: "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back." Because she is already dead and he must pass the note off as her own writing, he practices that exact sentence repeatedly — the seven identical lines are his successive handwritten drafts as he tries to disguise his handwriting and produce a convincing forgery. The closing line is his own resigned realization: his real handwriting cannot be disguised, so the very note he is practicing will betray him — he knows he is in trouble.

runs.latest_final: The killer murdered his wife and then forged a farewell note in her handwriting—"You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back"—so that her disappearance would look like she had voluntarily walked out on the marriage. To make the forgery convincing, he practiced copying her handwriting by writing the sentence over and over. Looking at the results of his practice, he sighs, "I know I'm in trouble," because the writing is clearly his own rather than hers and would expose the note as a forgery.
